2.1: Sanjaya, narrating to the blind king Dhritarashtra, describes Arjuna collapsed in grief on the battlefield — eyes full of tears, undone by pity for those he's about to fight. Krishna, addressed here as Madhusudana ("slayer of Madhu"), is about to answer him. The rest of the chapter is that answer.
2.2: Krishna's first words aren't comforting — they're a rebuke. This collapse, he says, is beneath Arjuna: unworthy of him, disgraceful, the kind of weakness that shuts the door to honor rather than opening it. Compassion has curdled into paralysis, and Krishna names it as such before offering anything else.
2.3: Krishna presses harder: don't give in to this weakness, it doesn't suit who you are. Shake off the faintheartedness and get up. He hasn't yet given a reason — first he simply insists that Arjuna is bigger than this moment.
2.4: Arjuna answers with the real difficulty: Bhishma and Drona aren't strangers on the other side — they're his elder and his teacher, people he owes reverence to. How does he aim an arrow at someone he's supposed to honor?
2.5: He'd rather beg for his food for the rest of his life than kill these teachers, he says. Any wealth or comfort won after killing them would come stained with their blood — a victory he couldn't actually enjoy.
2.6: Arjuna admits he doesn't even know which outcome is better — his side winning or losing — because the men arrayed against him are the very people he doesn't want to see dead. The war has stopped making sense to him from the inside.
2.7: Arjuna finally names what's happening to him — pity has overwhelmed his judgment, and he no longer knows where his duty lies. He drops the argument and asks directly: tell me plainly what's right, I'm your student, I've come to you for refuge. This is the moment the debate becomes teaching.
2.8: He adds that no prize would fix this — not an unrivaled kingdom, not even rule over the gods. The grief eating at him isn't about outcomes; it runs deeper than anything winning could touch.
2.9: Having said his piece, Arjuna goes quiet: "I will not fight." Ten verses of chapter 2 have built to this refusal — and only now, with Arjuna emptied out and asking to be taught, does Krishna begin to actually answer him.
2.10: Sanjaya notes a small, striking detail: as Krishna begins to speak to the despondent Arjuna between the two armies, he is smiling. The traditions hear that smile differently: Sivananda and others render it simply as a smile, even a gracious one; Śaṅkara and Rāmānuja hear an edge of ridicule in it — a jolt to shake Arjuna awake. Either way, the mood turns here: the teaching begins.
2.11: Krishna's actual teaching begins here, and it opens with a paradox: Arjuna is grieving over people who don't warrant grief, even while sounding wise. The wise, Krishna says, mourn neither the living nor the dead — because grief assumes something is truly lost, and that's exactly what's in question.
2.12: Krishna makes the claim directly personal: there was never a time he, Arjuna, or any of these kings did not exist, and there will never be a time they stop existing. Whatever happens on this battlefield, it isn't the end of anyone, in the sense that matters most.
2.13: Just as this same self moves through childhood, youth, and old age within one body without becoming someone new each time, it moves into another body at death the same way. The wise aren't troubled by that — it's a change of clothing, not a loss of the person.
2.14: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain — Krishna calls these the coming and going of the senses meeting the world. They arrive, they pass, none of them last; the instruction is simply to endure them without being ruled by them.
2.15: The person these fluctuations don't shake — who meets pleasure and pain with the same steadiness — is the one Krishna says is fit for what's imperishable. Steadiness under the ordinary ups and downs is the qualifying test, not withdrawal from them.
2.16: Krishna draws the line the rest of this section rests on: what is unreal never truly comes into being, and what is real never stops being. Seers, he says, have seen this distinction clearly — the task now is to know which category the self belongs to.
2.17: That which pervades everything, Krishna says — call it the indestructible — cannot be destroyed by anyone or anything. This is the "real" side of the line just drawn: not a thing among things, but what all things are made of or held within.
2.18: The bodies have an end, Krishna says plainly — that much is true and doesn't need arguing. But the self wearing them is eternal, indestructible, beyond measuring, and it's on that basis, not despite it, that he tells Arjuna to fight.
2.19: Anyone who thinks of the self as a killer, or as something that gets killed, hasn't understood it, Krishna says — the self itself neither slays nor is slain. Bodies act and are acted on; the self isn't in that category at all.
2.20: It is never born and never dies, Krishna says — it doesn't come into being and then someday go out of it. Unborn, eternal, ancient beyond reckoning, it isn't touched when the body it wore is destroyed.
2.21: If you truly know the self this way — indestructible, unborn, unchanging — Krishna asks, how could you be the one who kills, or the one killed? Violence to the body, in his logic, isn't violence to what a person actually is.
2.22: Krishna gives the image the whole chapter turns on: as a person sheds worn-out clothes for new ones, the embodied self sheds worn-out bodies for new ones. Death, on this account, is a change of clothing, not an ending.
2.23: No weapon can cut it, no fire burn it, no water soak it, no wind dry it out, Krishna says. He lists the ways the physical world destroys things, one by one, to show the self doesn't belong to that world at all.
2.24: He restates it as a summary: uncuttable, unburnable, unwettable, undryable — eternal, everywhere, stable, unmoving, ancient. This is less new information than the same claim driven home from every angle so it actually lands.
2.25: It's called unmanifest, unthinkable, unchangeable, Krishna says — beyond what the senses or even ordinary thought can grasp. Knowing this much, he tells Arjuna, grief simply doesn't fit the situation anymore.
2.26: Krishna then makes an unusual concession: even if you don't accept the argument above, even if you think of the self as being born and dying over and over, grief still isn't warranted. He covers the skeptic's objection without needing to win the metaphysical case first.
2.27: Because if birth happens, death is certain to follow, and if death happens, birth is certain to follow — that's simply how the cycle runs. Grieving over something completely inevitable, Krishna says, accomplishes nothing.
2.28: Every being is hidden before birth and after death, Krishna says — only the stretch in between, one lifetime, is visible to us. The traditions read this differently: Sankara takes "unmanifest" as the being's actual state outside a lifetime; Ramanuja reads it as simply unknown to us, not nonexistent. Either way, his question stands: what is there to grieve over in something this ordinary?
2.29: Some glimpse this self as a marvel, some describe it as a marvel, some hear about it as a marvel — and even after hearing, Krishna admits, hardly anyone actually grasps it. What he's teaching is hard to really take in, not just hard to explain.
2.30: This section closes where it started: the self dwelling in every body is permanently indestructible, so grief for any creature, on these grounds, doesn't hold up. Krishna has made his case for the self — the next question is what to actually do with it.
2.31: Krishna shifts from metaphysics to Arjuna's actual role: as a kshatriya, a warrior, there is no higher calling than a righteous war. This isn't yet the argument for acting without attachment — it's the simpler, prior point that this fight is his job.
2.32: A war like this, Krishna says, unsought and standing before Arjuna like an open door to heaven, is something a warrior should count himself lucky to be handed. He reframes the battle Arjuna dreads as an opportunity rather than a burden.
2.33: Refuse this fight, though, and it isn't neutral — Krishna says walking away from a duty this clear counts as wrongdoing, not caution. Arjuna's "better to do nothing" isn't the safe option he thinks it is.
2.34: People will talk about this refusal forever, Krishna warns, and for someone as respected as Arjuna, that kind of lasting disgrace is worse than dying. He appeals here to something concrete and human — reputation — not abstract philosophy.
2.35: The men who've admired him for his skill will read his withdrawal as simple fear, Krishna says, and he'll shrink in their eyes precisely because they held him in such high regard. The higher the esteem, the harder the fall.
2.36: His enemies, meanwhile, will mock his strength with insults that never should have been given the chance to be said — and Krishna asks what could hurt more than that. It's a blunt, almost unphilosophical appeal, sitting in the middle of the chapter's loftiest arguments.
2.37: Either way this goes, Krishna says, there's something to be gained: die, and heaven is his; win, and the earth is his. So — stand up, resolved to fight. It's the last practical argument before the teaching turns to how to fight.
2.38: Then comes the pivot: fight, yes, but hold pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal while doing it. That shift — acting without being gripped by the outcome — is what keeps the action itself from becoming wrongdoing, and it's the thread the rest of the chapter follows.
2.39: Krishna names what he's done so far — this has been the wisdom of understanding (Sankhya) — and now offers a second teaching, the wisdom of disciplined action (Yoga), which he says frees a person from action's usual grip. Understanding the self was step one; learning how to act from it is step two.
2.40: This practice has an unusual property, Krishna says — no effort spent on it is ever wasted, and it doesn't backfire. Even a small amount of it is enough to protect someone from real danger, which is a rare thing to say about a spiritual discipline.
2.41: On this path there's a single, unified resolve, Krishna says, while the minds of the undecided branch out endlessly, scattered in every direction at once. Clarity of purpose, not effort alone, is what he's pointing at here.
2.42: Krishna criticizes people who take only the ritual, reward-promising portions of scripture at face value — flowery language promising heaven, insisting "there is nothing else" beyond it. It's a warning against treating spiritual teaching as a transaction for future benefits rather than a real change of understanding.
2.43: Those caught up this way, he continues, are driven by desire and aimed at heaven, chasing elaborate rites for pleasure and power — and the pursuit, however impressive it looks, just leads back into more birth. It's activity that keeps a person inside the cycle it claims to escape.
2.44: People whose minds are absorbed this way in pleasure and status, Krishna says, never develop the single, settled resolve real practice needs — their attention stays scattered across outcomes instead of resting anywhere steady. The problem isn't desire being wrong exactly; it's that this kind of mind can't concentrate.
2.45: Scripture's ritual portions operate within the three basic qualities of nature, Krishna says — he asks Arjuna to stand above all three: free from opposites, settled in what's true, not preoccupied with acquiring or protecting things, anchored in the self instead. It's a call to outgrow religious transaction, not reject religion.
2.46: Once someone has that grounding, Krishna says, all the scripture in the world offers about as much as a small reservoir does to someone already standing in a flood. The teaching hasn't become false — it's just been outgrown, the way a map matters less once you've arrived.
2.47: This is the verse the chapter is best known for: you have a claim on the work itself, Krishna says, never on its results. Don't act for what you'll get — but don't use that as an excuse to do nothing either. Refusing to act is its own kind of attachment, just dressed as restraint.
2.48: Krishna defines the practice directly: act steadily, let go of attachment to how it turns out, and meet success and failure with the same composure. That evenness itself, he says, is what Yoga means here — not a technique, but a quality of mind carried into ordinary action.
2.49: Krishna ranks the two: action done for its rewards falls far short of action grounded in this settled mind, and he calls those driven by results genuinely miserable, however successful they look. The traditions read this differently: Sankara hears knowledge outranking action, action as a lesser path to be surpassed; Ramanuja hears one way of acting — with equanimity — outranking another way of acting, still done with attachment.
2.50: Someone acting this way, Krishna says, sheds the weight of both good deeds and bad ones — neither builds up as a debt to be carried. He sums up the whole teaching in a phrase: Yoga is skill in action, not withdrawal from it.
2.51: Those who act this way, Krishna says, give up the fruits their actions would otherwise produce and are freed from the whole cycle of being born again — they reach a state past all affliction. The reward for not chasing rewards turns out to be the deepest one available.
2.52: Once his mind gets past this confusion, Krishna tells Arjuna, he'll stop caring much about scripture already heard or still to come — not from disrespect, but because direct clarity makes secondhand instruction less urgent.
2.53: When his mind stops being pulled around by competing scriptural claims and simply rests steady in the self, Krishna says, that steadiness itself is the realization he's been describing. The goal isn't more information — it's an intellect that has stopped wobbling.
2.54: Arjuna asks the question that opens the chapter's final movement: what does someone with this steady wisdom — sthitaprajna, "one whose understanding stands firm" — actually look like? How do they talk, sit, move through the world? He wants the abstraction made into a recognizable person.
2.55: Krishna answers: someone who has let go of every desire arising in the mind, and finds contentment there without needing anything outside it, is what steady wisdom looks like. The traditions read this differently: Sankara hears contentment "in the self alone" — the mind resting in its own true nature; Ramanuja hears simple contentment with oneself, self-sufficiency without invoking a deeper merger.
2.56: It's someone whose mind doesn't buckle under hardship, doesn't chase after pleasures, and has worked clear of attachment, fear, and anger. Krishna is describing an even keel held in both directions — not shaken by loss, not grasping after gain.
2.57: Someone with no clinging attachment anywhere, who meets good fortune and bad without either delighting or recoiling — that person's wisdom is settled, Krishna says. The test keeps being the same one: can you meet both sides of experience the same way?
2.58: Krishna gives the image: like a tortoise pulling its limbs completely inside its shell, this person can draw the senses back from their objects at will. It's a capacity, not a permanent retreat — the tortoise can also put its limbs back out.
2.59: Restraint alone gets you partway, Krishna admits — the objects recede, but the taste for them, the underlying pull, can still linger. Only on seeing something higher does even that residual craving finally let go, which is why willpower by itself isn't the whole method.
2.60: He's honest about how hard this is: even a discerning person who's genuinely trying can have their mind forcibly swept away by the sheer turbulence of the senses. This isn't a verse for people who've already mastered themselves — it's a warning for people who think they have.
2.61: The answer to that difficulty, Krishna says, is to gather the senses in and hold steady with attention fixed on him — wisdom stays firm exactly to the degree the senses are under control. Restraint needs somewhere to rest its attention, not just something to resist.
2.62: Krishna traces how the fall actually starts: dwelling on an object breeds attachment to it, attachment breeds desire, and desire, when thwarted, breeds anger. It's a chain reaction that begins somewhere as ordinary as simply thinking about something too much.
2.63: He follows the chain to its end: anger clouds judgment, clouded judgment corrupts memory, corrupted memory destroys discrimination, and losing discrimination is ruin. Each link looks small alone — the danger is in how automatically one leads to the next.
2.64: The way out isn't avoiding the world, Krishna says — it's moving through it with senses free of both attraction and aversion, under one's own governance. Peace comes from that inner freedom, not from having fewer objects to encounter.
2.65: Once that peace is real, Krishna says, sorrow dissolves along with it, and a tranquil mind settles into steadiness quickly, almost as a natural consequence. Peace isn't the reward at the end of the practice — it's what makes the rest of it possible.
2.66: Without that inner integration, Krishna says, there's no real wisdom, no meditation worth the name, no peace, and — since peace is missing — no genuine happiness either. He lays out a dependency chain: pull one piece out and the rest collapses with it.
2.67: He returns to the image of vulnerability: a mind that follows the senses wherever they wander gets swept off course the way wind drags a boat across open water. Discrimination isn't lost through one dramatic failure — it's dragged away by drift.
2.68: So the practical conclusion, Krishna says, restates the whole section in one line: wisdom stays steady exactly where the senses are kept fully reined in from their objects. Nothing new here — just the argument brought back to its point.
2.69: Krishna offers a striking reversal: what looks like night to everyone else — the deeper reality most people are asleep to — is exactly where the self-controlled person is wide awake. And what the world stays busily awake chasing, the sage regards the way most people regard the middle of the night.
2.70: Peace belongs to the person desires can enter without disturbing, Krishna says — like an ocean that stays unmoved no matter how many rivers pour into it — not to someone who goes chasing after every desire that arises. The measure isn't having no desires; it's not being moved by the ones that come.
2.71: Letting go of desire itself, moving through life without craving, without the sense of "mine," without ego asserting itself — this, Krishna says, is what actually arrives at peace. Each phrase strips away one more layer of self-concern.
2.72: Krishna closes the chapter by naming this state itself: reach it, and delusion is over; hold it even to the moment of death, and it opens into the ultimate. The traditions read this last step differently: Sankara calls it identification with Brahman, the self realizing it always was that one reality; Ramanuja calls it attaining the Self, arriving at one's true nature in relation to Brahman without merging into it.
